This lesson gets you running Python code in your browser via Google Colab — nothing to install on your computer, nothing to configure, and so we'll be able to get going very quickly.

::: {.callout-note}
## If you have never written a line of code before
... this course assumes exactly that. Let me mention three things:

1. I don't think the best way to learn programming is to spend time trying to memorize the syntax; that will come naturally with experience. The best way to learn is to actually write and think about coding real problems. This page includes a lot of discussion of the syntax, but don't make flash cards about it or anything like that. We'll be writing programs soon enough, and you'll start to recognize the patterns the same way you do with spoken language.
2. There is hardly any cost for making a mistake in coding: the program gives an error, and you use the information in the error message to figure out how to fix your code. Students often try to write perfect code immediately, and want to give up if they can't. *Don't fall into that trap.* It is typical for a program to be "wrong" the first 5, 12, or 30 times you run it, and then you figure it out.
3. Some of your colleagues have some experience with coding, and they might have an easier time with this course (and may ask some advanced questions that I'll *try* to answer). Don't let that discourage you: I am creating this course with the beginner in mind, and so you will get all the information you need. That doesn't mean it will be easy — learning is always an uncomfortable process! But put forth the effort and you will be in a good place by December.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
What do I mean by "syntax"? A for loop in Python looks like `for i in items:`. That is, we need a `for`; a variable that changes every time through the "loop", `i`; the word `in`; then the list that the variable is drawn from, `items`; and then a colon `:`. This is "the syntax" for a for loop — forgetting any of those things will break the code.

In MATLAB, the syntax is `for i=items`. An equals sign `=` instead of `in`, no colon needed, and there also needs to be an `end` at the end of the block. The syntax varies from language to language, and if you switch between languages it can be confusing. But LLMs rarely mess up the syntax... they are a useful tool for getting started on a new project ("I need a python for loop that goes through a list of items"), translating between languages ("turn this python code into matlab code"), and debugging when your syntax is imperfect ("why is this producing an error?").
:::

## Google Colab: a lab bench in your browser

Go to [colab.research.google.com](https://colab.research.google.com) and sign in with your university Google account. Click **New notebook**. You now have a **notebook**: a document made of **cells**, where each cell holds a bit of Python code you can run by pressing **Shift+Enter** (or the ▶ button).

Type this into the first cell and run it — or, since this page runs Python **right here in your browser**, edit and run it below (the first run takes a few seconds while Python loads; after that it's instant):

```{pyodide}
print("hello, MCEN 1030")
```

The text should appear below the cell. The `print(...)` part is a **function** (a named, reusable action — much more on these in week 3) whose job is to display the thing between the quotes.

## Variables: giving numbers names

A **variable** is a name attached to a value, so you can use the value by its name:

```python
g = 9.81        # gravitational acceleration, m/s^2
h = 3.0         # drop height, m
```

::: {.column-margin}
The text after a `#` is a **code comment** — a note for humans that Python ignores. Here, we described the physical meaning of the variables and included the units. 
:::

Variable names can be simple or complex. Probably you will appreciate being able to write a simple, readable equation `y=0.5*g*t**2` later in your code, but we also could have defined `gravity_earth_surface = 9.81` and then used `y=0.5*gravity_earth_surface*t**2` later on. 

::: {.callout-tip}
It is good practice to make the variable names descriptive such that when you look at equations involving those variables, you know what is going on. Something like `g` in a mechanics-based program is probably fine, because we are so used to seeing `g` in our mechanics equations. But if we had some code that involved gravity on earth and gravity on the moon (for some reason), it is better to write those as `g_earth` and `g_moon` instead of `g_1` and `g_2`.
:::

The `=` sign here does **not** mean "equals" in the math sense. It means **"store the value under this name."** This structure conflicts with our experience with algebra, for example:

```python
count = count + 1
```

If we did algebra on this equation: subtract `count` from both sides, leaving `0=1`... nonsense. But as an instruction, it will take the (current) value of `count`, add `1`, and store the resulting value under the name `count` (thus replacing the old value). Perfectly acceptable, and indeed it is a common ingredient in code.


## A good habit to get into: predict, then run

Here is a complete little program. **Before you run it, write down what you expect it to display.**

```{pyodide}
g = 9.81
h = 3.0
t = (2 * h / g) ** 0.5
print(t)
```

(Sure, you can run it without thinking. I'm not keeping track of what you are doing here, but for the sake of your learning, I think you should think! Otherwise you're just watching a really boring TV show...)

::: {.column-margin}
`**` is Python's "raise to a power," so `x ** 0.5` is a square root. And `*` must always be written explicitly: `2h` will give an error; you need `2 * h` instead.
:::

Some reading help: line 3 computes $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$ — the fall time of a dropped object. So before running: $2 \times 3 / 9.81 \approx 0.61$, and $\sqrt{0.61} \approx 0.78$. Prediction: something near `0.78`.

Now run it. It should match, unless you changed something in the code. **Verification**!

## Errors are data

In the code above, change `t = (2 * h / g) ** 0.5` to `t = (2 * h_1 / g) ** 0.5`, and run it again. You'll get an angry red block ending in something like:

```
NameError: name 'h_1' is not defined
```

Two things to know about errors:

**They are normal.** Experts probably do make fewer errors, but they don't make zero errors... and actually, I use errors as a way to write code *faster*: just write out a sloppy version of the code without expecting it to work, then run, read and fix the error; run, read and fix the error; run, read and fix the error, and by then I'm probably done. *Read the error messages*, they usually describe the error and point to where it occurred in the code. Here: `NameError` because we used a variable name that the program didn't know, and it will point to line 3 of the code.

**They are the friendly failure mode.** It is way more difficult to figure out why code runs successfully, but produces a wrong answer. Error messages are kind of nice because they tell you exactly what is wrong (maybe cryptically)!

::: {.callout-tip}
Understanding error messages is a genuinely excellent use of an LLM: paste the code and the full error, and ask what's wrong. Verify the explanation makes sense — don't let the LLM do all your thinking for you!
:::

## Reading before writing

You now know enough to *read* simple Python. Predict what this displays before running:

```{pyodide}
a = 4
b = a * 2
a = 1
print(b)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Click for the answer
`8` — not `2`. Line 2 stored the *value* 8 under `b`; it did not create a live mathematical relationship "b is twice a." When `a` changed afterward, `b` is unaware. The code executes **top to bottom, once, each line acting on values as they are at that moment**.
:::

::: {.bring-to-class}
On paper, two things:

1. Your prediction for what this displays with one sentence of reasoning:
```python
x = 10
y = x + 5
x = x + 1
print(x)
print(y)
```

2. An electric toothbrush draws about 0.3 A of current ($I$) through 4 ohms of resistance ($R$); a space heater draws about 12 A through 10 ohms. On paper, set the current and resistance values in the first four lines of your code, then compute and print the power dissipated, $P = I^2 R$, for *both* devices. Don't forget to `#` comment! Write out your hand estimate on the side. Which device do you expect will dissipate more power?
:::
